title: Downloading and caching BODS GTFS data
text: Bus Open Data Service (BODS) provides timetable data bus services England regional GTFS zip files. files large — East Midlands zip around 600MB — downloading one every session impractical. bodsr2 solves simple caching layer. first call gtfs_load() downloads zip, parses tidytransit object, saves local cache. Subsequent calls load directly cache, dramatically faster.

title: Downloading and caching BODS GTFS data
text: typical connection takes around 40 seconds. second call much faster: cache stored platform’s user cache directory. can find gtfs_cache_dir(), clear gtfs_delete_cache("east_midlands"). cache automatically refreshed GTFS feed expires (indicated feed_end_date feed info). can also force fresh download time:
code: library(bodsr2)  gtfs <- gtfs_load("east_midlands") #> ℹ Downloading GTFS data for "east_midlands" from BODS. #> ℹ This file is large and may take a moment. #> ✔ Zip saved to ~/.cache/R/bodsr2/east_midlands.zip #> ℹ Reading GTFS zip for "east_midlands". This may take a moment. #> ✔ GTFS data cached to ~/.cache/R/bodsr2/east_midlands.rds gtfs <- gtfs_load("east_midlands") # completes in around 3 seconds gtfs <- gtfs_load("east_midlands", download = TRUE)

title: Downloading and caching BODS GTFS data
text: gtfs_load() returns tidygtfs object — named list tibbles, one GTFS table: standard tidytransit object. See tidytransit documentation full guide working . rest vignette shows one example illustrate kind analysis object supports.
code: names(gtfs) #>  [1] "agency"         "stops"          "routes"         "calendar"       #>  [5] "calendar_dates" "trips"          "shapes"         "feed_info"      #>  [9] "stop_times"

what: Example: services departing from Derby Bus Station Bay 4
title: Downloading and caching BODS GTFS data
text: V1 Villager service (Derby Burton-upon-Trent) departs Bay 4 Derby Bus Station. stop ID GTFS data "1090BSTN04": find services start stop, look trips stop appears lowest stop sequence number: Four routes use Bay 4: V1, TP, 70, 70A. trip_headsign column shows destination displayed front bus, informative route_long_name (always populated BODS GTFS data). V1 entries include outbound trips (Burton Wetmore) inbound trips terminating Derby Bus Station, since Bay 4 serves origin terminus route.
code: gtfs$stops |>   dplyr::filter(stop_id == "1090BSTN04") |>   dplyr::select(stop_id, stop_name, platform_code) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   stop_id    stop_name   platform_code #>   <chr>      <chr>       <chr>         #> 1 1090BSTN04 Bus Station 4 library(dplyr)  gtfs$stop_times |>   filter(stop_id == "1090BSTN04") |>   left_join(gtfs$trips, by = "trip_id") |>   left_join(gtfs$routes, by = "route_id") |>   distinct(route_short_name, trip_headsign) #> # A tibble: 9 × 2 #>   route_short_name trip_headsign             #>   <chr>            <chr>                     #> 1 V1               Derby Bus Station         #> 2 V1               Burton                    #> 3 V1               Burton Train Stn          #> 4 TP               Derby Bus Station (Bay 4) #> 5 70               Derby Bus Station         #> 6 70A              Derby Bus Station         #> 7 70A              Methodist Church          #> 8 V1               Wetmore                   #> 9 70A              Willington

what: Resolving the ping to a GTFS trip
title: Combining real-time location data with timetable data using bodsr2
text: SIRI-VM’s dated_vehicle_journey_ref field map directly GTFS identifier. Instead, resolve trip joining origin stop departure time, narrowing service running today’s date. First, convert UTC departure time local time, since GTFS stores departure times local clock time: Find candidate trips departing origin stop time: Three candidates — one per service pattern (weekday, Saturday, Sunday). Narrow trip running today’s date using calendar tables: One trip resolved. production application pre-compute active trips startup rather performing joins every poll.
code: dep_local <- hms::as_hms(format(   with_tz(bus$origin_aimed_departure_time, "Europe/London"),   "%H:%M:%S" ))  dep_date <- as.Date(with_tz(bus$origin_aimed_departure_time, "Europe/London")) day_col  <- tolower(as.character(wday(dep_date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)))  dep_local #> 14:05:00 dep_date #> [1] "2026-07-21" day_col #> [1] "monday" candidates <- gtfs$stop_times |>   filter(     stop_id        == bus$origin_ref,     departure_time == dep_local   ) |>   group_by(trip_id) |>   filter(stop_sequence == min(stop_sequence)) |>   ungroup()  nrow(candidates) #> [1] 3 active_services <- gtfs$calendar |>   filter(     .data[[day_col]] == 1,     as.Date(start_date) <= dep_date,     as.Date(end_date)   >= dep_date   ) |>   pull(service_id)  # Apply calendar_dates exceptions cancelled <- gtfs$calendar_dates |>   filter(as.Date(date) == dep_date, exception_type == 2) |>   pull(service_id)  added <- gtfs$calendar_dates |>   filter(as.Date(date) == dep_date, exception_type == 1) |>   pull(service_id)  active_services <- union(setdiff(active_services, cancelled), added)  trip <- gtfs$trips |>   filter(     trip_id    %in% candidates$trip_id,     service_id %in% active_services   )  trip |> select(trip_id, trip_headsign, direction_id) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   trip_id                                  trip_headsign direction_id #>   <chr>                                    <chr>                <int> #> 1 VJa02d83251371dbf1e4278cd05269c635c25416 Burton                   0

code: trip_stops <- gtfs$stop_times |>   filter(trip_id == trip$trip_id) |>   arrange(stop_sequence) |>   select(stop_sequence, stop_id, departure_time) |>   left_join(     gtfs$stops |> select(stop_id, stop_name, stop_lat, stop_lon),     by = "stop_id"   )  nrow(trip_stops) #> [1] 77

title: Combining real-time location data with timetable data using bodsr2
text: simple haversine distance calculation finds nearest stop vehicle’s current position: bus stop 40 77, near Balmoral Way Hatton, 33 metres stop.
code: haversine <- function(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) {   r <- 6371000   p <- pi / 180   a <- sin((lat2 - lat1) * p / 2)^2 +        cos(lat1 * p) * cos(lat2 * p) * sin((lon2 - lon1) * p / 2)^2   2 * r * asin(sqrt(a)) }  trip_stops <- trip_stops |>   mutate(dist_m = haversine(bus$latitude, bus$longitude, stop_lat, stop_lon))  nearest <- trip_stops |> slice_min(dist_m, n = 1)  nearest |> select(stop_sequence, stop_name, dist_m) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   stop_sequence stop_name    dist_m #>           <int> <chr>         <dbl> #> 1            40 Balmoral Way   32.8

title: Combining real-time location data with timetable data using bodsr2
text: next stop Lime Grove, timetabled 14:42.
code: next_stop <- trip_stops |>   filter(stop_sequence == nearest$stop_sequence + 1)  next_stop |> select(stop_sequence, stop_name, departure_time) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   stop_sequence stop_name  departure_time #>           <int> <chr>      <time> #> 1            41 Lime Grove 14:42:00

title: Combining real-time location data with timetable data using bodsr2
text: timetabled departure origin stop trip_stops. Comparing origin_aimed_departure_time SIRI-VM ping gives us delay: bus departed time. positive value indicates bus left late; negative value indicates left early — happen services, particularly later evening departures.
code: origin_timetabled <- trip_stops |>   filter(stop_sequence == min(stop_sequence)) |>   pull(departure_time)  actual_departure <- hms::as_hms(format(   with_tz(bus$origin_aimed_departure_time, "Europe/London"),   "%H:%M:%S" ))  delay_mins <- as.numeric(actual_departure - origin_timetabled, units = "mins")  cat("Delay:", delay_mins, "minutes\n") #> Delay: 0 minutes

text: R package accessing Bus Open Data Service (BODS), UK government’s open data platform bus location timetable data England. bodsr2 provides two things: real-time vehicle locations via SIRI-VM API using httr2, parsed tidy data frames suitable use tidyverse; caching layer BODS regional GTFS timetable files, designed feed directly tidytransit. data sources can combined support rich bus tracking timetable information. bodsr2 inspired bodsr Francesca Bryden (Department Transport). extends work httr2-based implementation, tidy tibble output, improved parameter handling tidytransit integration.

what: Notes on the BODS API feed
title: Call the Bus Open Data Service (BODS) API Through R
text: BODS API covers bus services England . Welsh Scottish operators included. feed may contain ghost buses - vehicles whose position data many hours old. Use filter_fresh() remove . unknown operator_ref silently ignored API, returns vehicles bounding box instead. get_siri_vm() warn supplied operator code appear results. BODS consumer rate limit one request per 5 seconds. Field availability varies operator. bearing, occupancy, destination_aimed_arrival_time optional SIRI-VM standard NA published.

title: Call the Bus Open Data Service (BODS) API Through R
text: BODS provides real-time vehicle location data two formats: SIRI-VM (XML) GTFS-RT (binary protobuf). bodsr2 uses SIRI-VM. GTFS-RT designed high-frequency, low-latency consumption suits city-wide transit displays. SIRI-VM richer per vehicle - response includes operator, origin, destination, bearing, aimed departure times - straightforward parse R. tracking small number specific vehicles known routes, SIRI-VM better choice. tracking every bus across large area real time, GTFS-RT appropriate. BODS provides timetable data two formats: TransXChange (XML) GTFS (zip CSV files). bodsr2 uses GTFS, primarily allows package build tidytransit rather parsing complex XML directly. GTFS files BODS converted TransXChange ITO World cover timetable content without meaningful loss data analysis purposes. bodsr Francesca Bryden (DfT) original R client BODS. uses GTFS-RT real-time data TransXChange timetables - opposite format choices bodsr2. valid approaches underlying data. bodsr2 inspired bodsr borrows name; fork official successor. UK2GTFS converts TransXChange UK transport formats GTFS. useful historical data sources predate BODS’s GTFS downloads. current BODS data, regional GTFS zips generally easier use directly. tidytransit provides tools working GTFS data R. bodsr2’s GTFS caching layer designed feed directly tidytransit - bodsr2 handles download caching, tidytransit handles analysis.
